details: 📅 Q4 · Unit 9 · Properties & Changes of Matter

opti.warm: Our film starts at an old Florida fort with a secret in its walls. First, inspect a strange rock from the coast.
opti.lesson: Today you're a materials scientist. Turn shells into stone, test two rocks, then climb a hardness ladder.

captions.text: Long ago, ships and armies fought over this little Florida town.
Spain built a stone fort to guard it.
Look closer. The walls are made of shells.
In 1740, enemy cannons fired at the fort for 27 days.
The cannonballs bounced off, or sank into the soft shell rock.
More than 300 years later, the walls still stand.
How do scientists describe and compare different kinds of matter?

words: Anything that takes up space and has mass. Solids, liquids, and gases are all matter.
A feature of an object you can observe or measure, like color, shape, or size.
How much matter is in an object. You measure mass with a balance or scale.
How much space an object takes up. A basketball has more volume than a tennis ball.
How the surface of an object feels: smooth, rough, bumpy, or soft.
How easily an object can be scratched. A diamond is very hard. Chalk is soft.

parts.title: What Is Matter?
parts.html:
Everything around you is made of matter: your desk, the water you drink, even the air you breathe. Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass.

Air is matter too. Blow up a balloon, and the air inside takes up space and pushes the sides out.

parts.title: Properties You Can Observe
parts.html:
A property is a feature you can observe or measure. You can see color, shape, and size. You can feel texture: smooth, rough, or bumpy.

Hardness tells how easily something can be scratched. A rock is hard. Clay and chalk are soft.

parts.title: Properties You Measure with Tools
parts.html:
Some properties need tools. A balance measures mass. A ruler measures length, and a measuring cup measures the volume of a liquid.

A thermometer measures temperature: how hot or cold something is, in degrees. Sand in the sun has a higher temperature than sand in the shade. Tools give exact numbers, so two scientists can compare what they found.

check.q: A friend says, "Air isn't matter. You can't even see it." What do you think?

options.t: Right. If you can't see it, it isn't matter.
options.miss: Think about a balloon. What fills it up and pushes its sides out?

options.t: Air is matter. It takes up space, like the air that fills a balloon, and it has mass.
options.ok: Yes! You can't see air, but it takes up space and has mass. That makes it matter.

compare.title: Which rock takes a hit?
compare.look: Two real rocks, each on a lit specimen tray. Specimen A is coquina, the Florida shell rock. Specimen B is granite, a hard rock made of tightly packed crystals. Under the trays are two model tests: a marble for a cannonball, and a cup of water.

trays.alt: Rough, cream-colored coquina packed with broken shells and tiny holes
trays.label: Specimen A

trays.alt: Smooth, speckled granite with pink, white, and black crystals
trays.label: Specimen B

ask.q: Which rock has shells you can see and tiny holes?
ask.ok: Yes. Specimen A is coquina, full of shells and holes.
ask.miss: Look closely. Which one is packed with broken shells?

ask.q: Which rock is hard and made of tightly packed, speckled crystals?
ask.miss: Look again. Which one has pink, white, and black specks?

compare.testDo: Put the marble under one tray and the water under the other: drag them, or tap one, then a tray. Press Run the test. Then swap.
compare.disclaimer: This is a model. Real cannonballs are much bigger and faster.

Amarble.text: The marble sinks in a little and stops. The soft, holey rock gives way and holds it.

Awater.text: The water soaks into the tiny holes between the shells.

Bmarble.text: The marble bounces off the hard granite with a crack.

Bwater.text: The water runs off the hard, tight surface.

compare.frame: This rock is ___, so the cannonball ___.

curator.A: Soft, holey rock → the cannonball sinks in. The wall soaks up the hit instead of cracking.
curator.B: Hard, tight rock → the cannonball bounces off. A big enough hit can crack hard, brittle rock.

compare.missFeat: Look at {label} again. Shells and holes, or tightly packed crystals?
compare.missClaim: Think about your test. Where did the marble sink in?
compare.done: Hardness and texture are properties. The fort's builders chose a rock whose properties fit the job.

after.alt: The fort's long gray stone walls behind a wooden bridge, with a flag flying above
after.html: No one knew how well shell rock would hold up against cannons, so the builders made the walls about 12 feet thick, and up to 19 feet on the ocean side. In 1740, the cannonballs bounced off or sank in a few inches.

wall.look: A model ladder of four real minerals, from soft at the top to hard at the bottom. A mineral is a natural solid, like the crystals in rocks. Each step has a real photo. The brass dial on the left shows each mineral's hardness number, from 1 (softest) to 10 (hardest).

predict.q: Can your fingernail scratch every mineral?
options: Yes, a fingernail can scratch any mineral
No, some minerals are too hard
predict.mine: Your prediction: {p}. Let's climb the ladder and find out.
predict.confirm: You predicted some minerals are too hard. The evidence agrees: a fingernail only scratches the softest ones, like talc.
predict.change: You predicted a fingernail could scratch anything. The evidence changed that idea: it only scratches the softest minerals, like talc.

wall.rule: Hardness is a property you can test. A harder material scratches a softer one. Scientists compare minerals by trying to scratch them, from talc (1) to diamond (10).

mix.q: A big, puffy pillow and a small rock sit side by side. A student says, "The pillow is bigger, so it has more mass." Is that right?

options.t: Yes. Bigger things always have more mass.
options.miss: Think about lifting each one. Size and mass are different properties.

options.t: No. The pillow has more volume, but the small rock has more mass.
options.ok: Yes! Volume is how much space something takes up. Mass is how much matter is in it. They are different properties.

wow.title: 27 days of cannon fire
wow.alt: The star-shaped stone fort beside the bay, with green lawns around it, seen from the air
wow.caption: Castillo de San Marcos from the air
wow.html:
In 1740, a British army fired cannons at the fort for 27 days. The coquina walls held.

The fort was finished in 1695 and was never captured in battle. Park rangers still fire its cannons today, as a show for visitors.
wow.insetCap: Rangers in old uniforms fire a cannon for visitors.

keyIdea: Every object is made of matter and has properties that scientists can observe and measure, like mass, volume, color, texture, hardness, and temperature. Scientists use properties to describe objects, compare them, and choose the right material for a job.

quiz.q: What is a property of matter?

options.t: A feature you can observe or measure, like color, texture, or mass
options.ok: 🌲 That is right! A property is something you can observe or measure about an object.

options.t: The place where an object is found
options.miss: Not quite. Think about what you can see, feel, or measure about an object. That is a property.
Not quite. Think about what you can see, feel, or measure about an object. That is a property.

quiz.q: Two students pick up a rock and a sponge. The rock feels much heavier. What property is different?

options.miss: Think again. When something feels heavier, it has more of which property? Hint: it starts with M.

options.ok: 🌲 Yes! The rock has more mass than the sponge. That is why it feels heavier.

options.miss: Think again. When something feels heavier, it has more of which property? Hint: it starts with M.

quiz.q: Which tool would a scientist use to measure the mass of an object?

options.miss: A ruler measures length and a thermometer measures temperature. Which tool measures how heavy something is?
A ruler measures length and a thermometer measures temperature. Which tool measures how heavy something is?

options.ok: 🌲 Exactly! A balance or scale measures mass: how much matter is in an object.
